name: Private Eye Cyclops crossword No 820
preamble: Running clockwise round the shaded squares from the top LH corner is part of a 2025 Poetry Corner tribute. The poem’s subject and their occupation are the answers to 36 & 37 and 44 across. The unchecked letters of the quote are listed below, except for the four that are revealed in the grid. A A A C C D D D D E E H H H I I I I I K M N N O O O O O O O P R R R R S S S S S T T T U U W Y Y

solutions.check: 78 entries verified against the grid image (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); the unclued ring is unsolved: no quotation in the post fits it

clue.text: Hairy miser involved with row about nothing

indicators.note: things that are involved are tangled together, so the letters get mixed up
to be about something is to go round it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A shaggy old skinflint gets into an argument over nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' reads as a description of the miser, but it is the definition in its slang sense of alarming or nerve-racking.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy is informal for frightening or dangerous, so a hairy moment is one that causes anxiety.

clue.text: Establishment pledges to replace love with ecstasy

indicators.note: to replace one thing with another is to swap it out for a new letter in the same spot

blocks.note: pledges are promises
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like O
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A business swaps romantic vows for a drug-fuelled high.
explanation.walkthrough: The O of the pledges is swapped for E, leaving PREMISES.
explanation.definitionFit: Premises are the building and grounds a business occupies, so the word can stand for the establishment itself.

clue.text: BoJo’s, um… about to drop round for “Big things”

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so a letter is removed
turned about means moved around, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: BoJo is the nickname of Boris Johnson, taken with its S
taken as written
a round shape is the letter O; this one is dropped

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, um-ing and ah-ing, is about to call round on some big beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: BoJo is the press nickname for former Prime Minister Boris Johnson. One O is removed from BOJOS plus UM, and the six letters left are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumbos are very large things, especially jumbo jets or elephants, after Jumbo the famous circus elephant.

clue.text: Like a pitch made by Conservative whip in uniform

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
to tan someone's hide is to whip or thrash them
uniform and regular both mean even or consistent

explanation.surface: A pitch, as in a sales pitch, delivered by a Tory party whip wearing uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a sales pitch or a political whip's pitch, but it is a sports field. A party whip enforces discipline among MPs, which disguises the verb sense of whip.
explanation.definitionFit: Football and cricket fields are laid out as oblongs with four right-angled corners, which is what rectangular describes.

clue.text: A Fabian arsehole rubbished Mayfair?

definitions.note: a definition by example, flagged by the question mark

indicators.note: something rubbished is trashed and wrecked, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rude Fabian socialist sneers at the posh London district of Mayfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society is a left-wing think tank, which suits a sneer at Mayfair, a wealthy district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayfair is one example of a smart, expensive, sought-after neighbourhood, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Cover for nut out cavorting on piss

indicators.note: cavorting means prancing about wildly, so the letters jump into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
both are slang for urine

explanation.surface: A drunk lunatic out on the piss needs some kind of cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' looks like a madman but it is slang for the head. 'On the piss' is British slang for out drinking heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpiece worn over a bald patch literally covers the head, and nut is slang for the head.

clue.text: In which civil servants work to insert line in an area near the genitals

indicators.note: to insert is to put something into the middle of something else

blocks.note: the pubic region is the area around the genitals
L is a standard abbreviation for line
a sector is an area or zone

explanation.surface: Civil servants are told to draw a line somewhere rather intimate.
explanation.walkthrough: The anatomical phrase is a pubic sector; putting L inside the first word changes it into the part of the economy run by the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Civil servants are government employees, and the government-run part of the economy is called the public sector.

clue.text: A part of Clinton (stag!) enjoyed giving a performance

indicators.note: a part of a phrase is a piece cut out of its running letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton on a stag night, enjoying himself while showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets and exclamation mark break up the phrase so the run of letters is hard to spot. 'Enjoyed' serves both in the letter run and as a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who is on stage is in front of an audience, actively delivering a show.

clue.text: Text (not Trump’s first): HAND OVER ZELENSKY’S BUTT

indicators.note: leaving out the first letter of a name chops a letter from the start of the word
a butt is the thick end of something, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written; its opening T is the one removed
to remit money is to hand it over
the final letter of the Ukrainian president's name

explanation.surface: A message, styled like a Trump capital-letter post, demanding that Zelensky hand over his backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals mimic Trump's social-media style. 'Trump's first' is T, taken from TEXT. 'BUTT' does double duty: it picks the last letter and is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A butt is the end part of something, such as a rifle butt, and an extremity is a far end.

clue.text: Decline to visit the Dobermans?

blocks.note: first meaning: to deteriorate or fall into ruin
second meaning, taken literally: to go and see some dogs

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is read literally for the second meaning; the question mark flags the joke. In Britain going to the dogs can also mean an evening at greyhound racing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to deteriorate badly, and taken word for word it describes a trip to see some hounds.

clue.text: Playful, perverted life, Epstein, finally

indicators.note: something perverted is twisted out of its proper shape, so the letters are scrambled
finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A grim aside on the depraved life and end of Jeffrey Epstein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playful' seems at odds with the dark surface, which hides that it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin means like an elf: small, delicate and mischievous, which matches playful or impish.

clue.text: Right to ditch Latin base

indicators.note: to ditch something is to throw it away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: something right and legal is lawful
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A justification for dropping Latin from the basic curriculum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like the definition, but it is the wordplay; the definition is 'base' in its sense of low or contemptible.
explanation.definitionFit: Base means morally low or worthless, and awful describes something very bad or dreadful in the same way.

clue.text: Perseverance of Sun once seat is lost

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper keeps on trying even after its candidate loses a parliamentary seat.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid famous for backing election winners; 'lost' reads as a lost seat but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenaciousness is the quality of holding on firmly and not giving up, which is exactly what perseverance means.

clue.text: Bloody American?

blocks.note: surface reading: a violent or wounded person from the USA
setter's reading: the swear word an American would use where a Briton says bloody

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like an adjective describing a person, but it is a British intensifying curse, and the clue asks for its American counterpart.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild expletives used for emphasis; the American one is the usual US equivalent of the British curse.

clue.text: Row about government leader’s cat

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round the other
a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: a tier is a row, as in tiers of seats
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A spat over the Prime Minister's cat, such as Larry at Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests an argument but here means a line of seats. Downing Street has an official cat, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiger is the largest of the big cats, a striped member of the feline family.

clue.text: (& 37.) [see preamble] That is covered by Private Eye lark?

indicators.note: something covered by another sits beneath it, so in the answer it comes after the covering piece

blocks.note: dick is old American slang for a private detective, a private eye
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, meaning that is
a lark is a small songster, a feathered creature
an instruction to the solver, not wordplay: the preamble supplies the definition

explanation.surface: A cheeky aside that the joke is being covered by Private Eye magazine itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private Eye' looks like the magazine that prints this puzzle, but it means a detective. The preamble says this is the poem's subject: Dickie Bird, the much-loved English cricket umpire who died in 2025.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this answer the subject of a Poetry Corner tribute, so the name is defined by the puzzle's theme rather than by clue words.

clue.text: see 36ac.
Scruffy figure surprisingly cares about rank

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is not the expected one, so the letters land in an unexpected order

blocks.note: taken as written
C stands for circa, Latin for about
a rank is a row or line, as in ranks of soldiers

explanation.surface: A dishevelled person turns out, against expectation, to be preoccupied with status.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a joining word but supplies a letter as the abbreviation c. for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A scarecrow is a figure dressed in old clothes to frighten birds, and its shabby look is the byword for scruffiness.

clue.text: Former Starmer residence – “No bearing on where your taxes go”

indicators.note: no means none of something, so the following item is left out of the word

blocks.note: ex- means former
Chequers is the country house in Buckinghamshire used by British Prime Ministers
a bearing is a compass direction, here south; it is removed

explanation.surface: A jibe that a past Prime Minister's grand house has nothing to do with public spending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former Starmer residence' reads as one idea, but 'Former' stands apart. 'No bearing' looks like an idiom for irrelevance; it takes S off the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exchequer is the British government department and national account that receives public revenue, including taxes.

clue.text: (& 21 dn.) Extended tip for candidates to be whittled down

blocks.note: extended means lengthy
to tip or lean over to one side, as a ship does when it heels

explanation.surface: A lengthy tip-off about which candidates should be cut from the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' suggests a piece of advice, but it is the verb meaning to lean, as a ship lists.
explanation.definitionFit: A longlist is the first wide selection for a prize or job, later trimmed down to a shortlist.

clue.text: [see preamble] “In Trump I reside”

indicators.note: the word sits inside the following phrase, so its letters lie within it

blocks.note: the letters run from inside the first word, through the second, into the third
an instruction to the solver, not wordplay: the preamble supplies the definition

explanation.surface: Trump announces where he lives, as if speaking from inside himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says this answer is the occupation of the poem's subject: Dickie Bird was a famous Test cricket umpire.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble asks for the subject's job, and Dickie Bird was renowned as an international cricket match official.

clue.text: Guide – mine’s protecting left ball

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it on all sides, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine
L is the abbreviation for left
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A guide warns about a mine shaft guarding a stray ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine's' looks like a possessive pronoun, but mine is the noun for a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot guides ships into harbour or steers an aircraft, and to pilot is to guide.

clue.text: It helps with DIY boob (look around inside)

indicators.note: moved around means shifted about, so the letters change places
inside means within, so one piece is placed in the middle of the other

blocks.note: tit is slang for a breast, as is boob
taken as written

explanation.surface: A home-improvement blunder where someone should have checked the work first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boob' reads as a mistake, which suits DIY, but it is the slang for a breast. DIY is do-it-yourself home repair.
explanation.definitionFit: A toolkit is a set of tools kept together, which is what helps a person doing their own home repairs.

clue.text: Sperm’s going so sloppy, so blathers

indicators.note: something sloppy is messy and careless, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken as written, with its S
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Crude chatter about bodily fluids, which itself is idle blather.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'so' is part of the letters; the second is a joining word. 'Blathers' looks like a verb but is a plural noun for chatterers.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip-mongers spread idle talk and rumour, and a blather is someone who talks long-windedly about nothing.

clue.text: Range of Coulson broadcast?

indicators.note: something broadcast goes out over the airwaves to be heard, not seen

blocks.note: Andy Coulson is the former News of the World editor who became David Cameron's press chief

explanation.surface: A question about how wide a reach a former tabloid editor's broadcasts had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests reach, but it is a mountain range. Coulson's first name, said with a possessive, matches the mountains' name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the long mountain range running down the western side of South America.

clue.text: No way to get inside – awful

indicators.note: getting inside something means entering it, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: nay is an old word for no
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Locked out with no way in, which is a dreadful situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No way' reads as one phrase of refusal, but it splits into two separate parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasty and awful are near synonyms, both meaning very unpleasant or bad.

clue.text: Search for something to watch – guide on small fur balls?

indicators.note: to balls something up is to make a mess of it, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: to channel is to direct or guide
S is the abbreviation for small
taken as written

explanation.surface: Looking for a TV guide to something about little furballs, such as kittens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guide' suggests a TV listings guide, which suits the surface, but it is the verb. 'Fur balls' reads as one thing, but 'balls' is the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To channel-surf is to flick rapidly between television stations looking for a programme worth viewing.

clue.text: Republic is inane, changing to accommodate party

indicators.note: changing means altering form, so the letters are rearranged
to accommodate a guest is to take them in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A political complaint that a republic is foolish yet adapts to suit a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' fits the political surface, but it is a social do.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia is a country in South-East Asia with an elected president, so it is a republic.

clue.text: So you’ll have to rest your plate on your lap? Extraordinary!

definitions.text: So you’ll have to rest your plate on your lap?

blocks.clueFragment: So you’ll have to rest your plate on your lap?
blocks.note: first meaning, split as two words
second meaning: remarkable, worthy of notice

explanation.surface: A host apologises that there is nowhere to put the dinner plates, which is quite something.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning splits the answer into NO TABLE; the question mark signals that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Notable describes something remarkable enough to be noticed, and having no table explains eating off one's lap.

clue.text: Kyiv hardline nuts booze

indicators.note: something nuts is crazy and out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hardliners in Ukraine's capital are going crazy and hitting the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' could be read as a noun for fanatics, but it is the mixing signal; 'booze' is the definition used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To booze is informal for consuming large amounts of alcohol, so the verb phrase matches it.

clue.text: One pathetic cut on a large material

indicators.note: something pathetic is a sorry, feeble mess, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: a means one, as in a single item
taken as written
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A tailor makes one poor cut into a big piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' looks like cloth, which suits the tailoring surface, but it is the adjective meaning real or substantial.
explanation.definitionFit: Material can mean real and physical rather than imaginary, and actual means existing in fact.

clue.text: Reform main party? Unreal, against Westminster norms!

indicators.note: to reform something is to form it again, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gibe that Reform UK calling itself the main party is fantasy, and improper in the Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: Reform UK is Nigel Farage's party, so 'Reform' reads as a name; it is the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Unparliamentary language or behaviour breaks the rules of conduct in the House of Commons at Westminster.

clue.text: Say “M” is very dismissive of victory, real sad type

definitions.note: phrase used as a noun: a thoroughly gloomy person

indicators.note: dismissing something means sending it away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: to utter is to say
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; its V is removed
V is the abbreviation for victory, as in V-sign

explanation.surface: The spymaster M in James Bond is scornful of success, a real downer.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the head of MI6 in the Bond films, which makes the letter look like a character. A misery is British slang for a moaner.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter means complete or real, and a misery is informal for a gloomy, complaining person.

clue.text: Did some dogging? Sounds quite virtuous!

indicators.note: sounds means the clue is judged by its pronunciation rather than spelling

blocks.note: chaste means pure and virtuous

explanation.surface: A cheeky joke that someone caught dogging claims to have been entirely pure.
explanation.walkthrough: Dogging is British slang for public sex; here it means dogging someone's footsteps, following them.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them persistently, so doing some dogging means pursuing someone.

clue.text: Has a spell behind bars – rabbits on about “item”

indicators.note: turned about means moved around, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: does are female rabbits
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prisoner serving a sentence keeps rabbiting on about some item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbits on' is British slang for chattering endlessly; here the rabbits are animals, with 'on' as a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time is the idiom for serving a prison sentence, which is a spell behind bars.

clue.text: Celeb for each child? Decline

blocks.note: per means for each, as in per person
a son is a child
to age is to decline with the years

explanation.surface: A celebrity is asked to visit every child and refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' suggests refusing an invitation, but it is the verb for growing older and weaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A personage is an important or distinguished person, which is near to a celebrity or celeb.

clue.text: Due to UFO con act? No, stupid!

indicators.note: something stupid makes no sense as it stands, so the letters must be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a flying-saucer sighting was a hoax, and is told off for being daft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, stupid!' reads as a retort, but 'No' belongs with the letters and 'stupid' is the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases introduce a cause or reason, so because of, owing to and on account of are interchangeable.

clue.text: Fashion again produces some fresh aperitif

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only a portion of it, a run taken from within its letters

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Reinventing a fashion look by mixing a fresh pre-dinner drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like the noun for clothing trends, but it is the verb meaning to shape or make.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion is to form or shape, so fashioning again means forming into a new shape.

clue.text: Herb grabs Virginia – and Lily?

definitions.note: a surname by example: the drag character Lily Savage

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: sage is a cooking herb
VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia

explanation.surface: A man called Herb seizes a woman named Virginia, and maybe Lily too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' and 'Virginia' look like people's names. Lily Savage was the brash drag persona of the British comedian Paul O'Grady.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily is the first name of the drag character whose surname completes the clue, a definition by association marked by the question mark.

clue.text: Absurdly, truly mad to host ball as an ethical obligation

indicators.note: absurdly means in a ridiculous, senseless way, so the letters are jumbled
a host takes in guests, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it's insane to feel bound by conscience to throw a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' suggests a dance, but it supplies the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral duty is something one is bound to do by conscience rather than law, which is an ethical obligation.

clue.text: Approval of Riot Act if in a muddle

indicators.note: a muddle is a confused jumble, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Parliament signs off the Riot Act even though the matter is confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a muddle' reads as one phrase, but 'in a' belongs with the letters. The Riot Act was a British law of 1714 for dispersing unruly crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratification is the formal confirmation of an agreement or law, which amounts to official approval.

clue.text: Nasty singular match, barrier to getting financial aid?

blocks.note: mean means unkind or nasty
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: A grim one-off contest stands between applicants and help with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'unusual', which fits nasty, but it is the grammar term giving one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A means test checks someone's income and savings before benefits are granted, so it can block access to state support.

clue.text: Somewhat hasty litigious writers

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the phrase is taken

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Authors who are rather quick to sue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' suggests authors, which suits the litigious surface, but means writing tools.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylus is a pointed instrument for writing on wax tablets, and the plural of that tool is styli.

clue.text: Balls up by north-eastern Republicans – a beauty!

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: nuts is slang for testicles, as is balls
NE is the abbreviation for north-eastern
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Republicans in the north-east have made a mess of things, ironically called a beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls up' reads as the British slang for a botch, but splits into a word and a direction signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stunner is an informal word for a very attractive person or thing, a real beauty.

clue.text: Small flag attached to chemists, a symbol of fascism?

blocks.note: a jack is a small flag flown at a ship's bow
Boots is a major British chain of pharmacies

explanation.surface: A little flag stuck to a pharmacy might hint at far-right sympathies.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots is the high-street pharmacy chain found in every British town.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackboots are tall military boots worn by Nazi soldiers, and they stand for authoritarian oppression.

clue.text: Wear them in winter when love-struck, head to toe

definitions.note: a description: the things you wear in winter

indicators.note: moving from head to toe sends the top letter to the bottom of the word

blocks.note: smitten means infatuated, struck by love

explanation.surface: Advice to wrap up warm in winter, especially when lovesick, from head to foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head to toe' reads as dressing from top to bottom; in a down clue it moves the first letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Mittens are thumbed gloves without separate fingers, worn on the hands in cold weather.

clue.text: Maybe old man‘s for health reforms

indicators.note: something that reforms takes a new shape, so the letters are reorganised

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly man is in favour of changes to the health service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' looks like an elderly person, but it is British slang for a husband or partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's other half is their spouse or partner, and old man is informal for a husband, one example.

clue.text: Cricketer‘s crusty member

blocks.note: crusty and short both mean curt and irritable
a leg is a limb, or member

explanation.surface: A cricketer has a grumpy limb, fitting the puzzle's cricket theme.
explanation.walkthrough: Short leg is a cricket fielding position close to the batter on the leg side, and also the fielder in it.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the fielder who stands in a position is named after it, so short leg is a player.

clue.text: Subject to chucking ball at hunks endlessly

indicators.note: chucking means throwing away, so a letter is discarded
without an end, a word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
a ball is round, like the letter O; it is thrown out
he-men are muscular hunks

explanation.surface: Someone is exposed to having a ball thrown at muscle men without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject to' reads as one phrase meaning liable to, but 'Subject' is the definition and 'to' is wordplay. 'At' simply joins the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main topic of a talk or piece of writing, which is its subject.

clue.text: See 43ac.
Pad out and measure regal bust

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are broken up and reset

blocks.note: an en is a printer's unit of width
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dressmaker adds padding and takes the measurements of a queen's chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a chest measurement, which suits the tailoring surface, but it is the mixing signal; 'and' joins the definition to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To pad out something is to make it bigger by adding material, which is to enlarge it.

clue.text: Neurotic, unstable bosses Cyclops has

indicators.note: something unstable will not hold its form, so the letters shift

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter Cyclops speaking of himself would say I've, I have

explanation.surface: The setter complains that he has anxious, erratic managers.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the puzzle's setter, so 'Cyclops has' becomes the first-person I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsessive describes a mind fixated on one thing, a trait commonly linked with neurotic anxiety.

clue.text: Balls squeezing middle of penis, so expire?

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to press it in from both sides, so one piece is held inside
the middle is the centre point, so the central letter is kept

blocks.note: Ed Balls is the former Labour cabinet minister turned TV presenter
the central letter of the five

explanation.surface: A crude joke about testicles crushing a member hard enough to be fatal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like slang for testicles, but it is the surname of the politician Ed Balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To end is to come to a close or finish, and expire means the same, like a licence running out.
